scenes.line1: Why does .NET split memory into layers?
scenes.say: Ever wonder why .NET splits memory into generations, and what happens with really big objects?

scenes.label: Generations
scenes.sub: Gen 0 is for short-lived objects. Gen 2 is for long-lived ones.
scenes.say: In .NET, Gen zero is for short-lived objects. Gen two is for long-lived ones. This keeps memory cleanup fast.

rows.b: Stored in the Large Object Heap

scenes.say: If an object is bigger than eighty-five kilobytes, it lands in the Large Object Heap. This area is only cleaned up during Gen two collections, and it isn’t compacted by default.
For example, if you allocate a one hundred kilobyte byte array, it goes straight to the Large Object Heap.

scenes.question: Does LOH get compacted every GC?
scenes.right: No, LOH is only collected in Gen 2 and is not compacted by default. This can cause fragmentation.
scenes.say: Here's a common trap: people think the Large Object Heap is compacted every time garbage collection runs. It's not. That can lead to fragmentation.
